package list

// This file is copied into a generated project by v1.assertListBindingProbe and
// run there as core/repository/list/list_binding_probe_test.go, with __MODULE__
// replaced by the generated module path.
//
// It exists because `?q=O'Brien` returned 502 in production. The list query
// builder used to write every filter VALUE into the statement text, so the
// apostrophe closed the SQL string literal and the remainder of the value became
// syntax the engine rejected. A name is not an attack; the same hole answers to
// `'; DROP TABLE ...; --`.
//
// The contract pinned here is one sentence: no byte a caller sends ever reaches
// the SQL TEXT. Every filter value is bound and referenced by a placeholder, the
// placeholders agree with the argument list in count and in order, and the value
// arrives at the driver with its type and its bytes intact.
//
// The probe lives in the list package itself so it can call the unexported
// placeholder() and derive the dialect's bind marker rather than hardcoding one
// — the same source runs unchanged against the MySQL and the PostgreSQL flavour
// of the generated builder.

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"go.einride.tech/aip/filtering"
	"go.einride.tech/aip/ordering"

	main_entity "__MODULE__/entity/all_types"
)

// probeRequest is the smallest thing satisfying ListRequest: a parsed filter,
// its declarations, and a fixed page. No order-by and no joins — neither binds
// anything, and both would only add text this probe would have to look past.
type probeRequest struct {
	filter       filtering.Filter
	declarations *filtering.Declarations
}

func (r probeRequest) GetFilter() filtering.Filter                       { return r.filter }
func (r probeRequest) GetFilteringDeclarations() *filtering.Declarations { return r.declarations }
func (r probeRequest) GetEnumValues() map[string]map[string]int64        { return nil }
func (r probeRequest) GetOrderBy() ordering.OrderBy                      { return ordering.OrderBy{} }
func (r probeRequest) GetPageSize() int32                                { return 10 }
func (r probeRequest) GetOffset() int64                                  { return 0 }
func (r probeRequest) GetJoinParams() *JoinParams                        { return nil }
func (r probeRequest) GetIncludeFields() []string                        { return nil }
func (r probeRequest) GetExcludeFields() []string                        { return nil }

// filterString carries the raw filter expression into filtering.ParseFilter,
// which is what a transport's list params type does.
type filterString string

func (f filterString) GetFilter() string { return string(f) }

// probeDeclarations declares the four fields these assertions filter on, in the
// same style rest/templates/handler_list_entity.go.tmpl emits: the standard
// functions, the true/false idents, and one DeclareIdent per field with the
// aip type its field type maps to.
func probeDeclarations(t *testing.T) *filtering.Declarations {
	t.Helper()
	declarations, err := filtering.NewDeclarations(
		filtering.DeclareStandardFunctions(),
		filtering.DeclareIdent("true", filtering.TypeBool),
		filtering.DeclareIdent("false", filtering.TypeBool),
		filtering.DeclareIdent("t07_varchar_req", filtering.TypeString),
		filtering.DeclareIdent("t02_integer_req", filtering.TypeInt),
		filtering.DeclareIdent("t03_float_req", filtering.TypeFloat),
		filtering.DeclareIdent("t26_datetime_req", filtering.TypeTimestamp),
	)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("building filter declarations: %v", err)
	}
	return declarations
}

// parseListRequest builds a ListRequest the way a transport does: through
// filtering.ParseFilter, so the value passes the real lexer, parser and type
// checker before it reaches the query builder. A hand-built AST would skip
// exactly the layers that have to carry an apostrophe intact.
func parseListRequest(t *testing.T, filter string) ListRequest {
	t.Helper()
	declarations := probeDeclarations(t)
	parsed, err := filtering.ParseFilter(filterString(filter), declarations)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("ParseFilter(%q): %v", filter, err)
	}
	return probeRequest{filter: parsed, declarations: declarations}
}

// buildProbeQuery builds the list query for a filter, failing the test if the
// builder rejects it.
func buildProbeQuery(t *testing.T, filter string, onlyCount bool) (string, []any) {
	t.Helper()
	query, args, err := New().BuildListEntityQuery(
		context.Background(),
		parseListRequest(t, filter),
		main_entity.AllTypes{},
		onlyCount,
	)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("BuildListEntityQuery(%q): %v", filter, err)
	}
	return query, args
}

// countPlaceholders counts the bind markers in a built query. MySQL's markers
// are all identical, so occurrences are the count; Postgres numbers them, so the
// count is how many consecutive ordinals appear. (No query here binds ten or
// more values, so "$1" cannot be matched as a prefix of "$10".)
func countPlaceholders(query string) int {
	if placeholder(1) == placeholder(2) {
		return strings.Count(query, placeholder(1))
	}
	n := 0
	for i := 1; strings.Contains(query, placeholder(i)); i++ {
		n++
	}
	return n
}

// ordinalPlaceholders reports whether the dialect numbers its markers, i.e.
// whether the ORDER the builder binds in is observable in the text.
func ordinalPlaceholders() bool { return placeholder(1) != placeholder(2) }

// probeFilters is every filter this file builds a query from. TestNoByteSlice
// Arguments sweeps the whole set, so anything added below belongs here too.
var probeFilters = []string{
	`t07_varchar_req = "O'Brien"`,
	`t07_varchar_req : "O'Brien"`,
	`t07_varchar_req = "'; DROP TABLE all_types; --"`,
	`t07_varchar_req : "' OR '1'='1"`,
	`t07_varchar_req = "x" AND (t02_integer_req = 3 OR t07_varchar_req = "z")`,
	`t26_datetime_req > timestamp("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z")`,
	`t26_datetime_req > "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"`,
	`t07_varchar_req : "50%"`,
	`t03_float_req > 0.000000123`,
	`t03_float_req > 3`,
}

// TestApostropheInFilterValueIsBound is the direct regression test for the
// reported failure: `?q=O'Brien` reached the SQL text and closed the string
// literal, and the endpoint answered 502.
func TestApostropheInFilterValueIsBound(t *testing.T) {
	const value = "O'Brien"
	query, args := buildProbeQuery(t, `t07_varchar_req = "`+value+`"`, false)

	if strings.Contains(query, value) {
		t.Errorf("the filter value is in the SQL text:\n%s", query)
	}
	// An odd number of single quotes is the signature of the bug: the value's
	// apostrophe leaves one literal open and everything after it is parsed as
	// SQL. Zero is what a fully bound query has.
	if n := strings.Count(query, "'"); n%2 != 0 {
		t.Errorf("SQL carries %d single quotes (odd — a string literal is left open):\n%s", n, query)
	}
	if len(args) != 1 {
		t.Fatalf("got %d arguments, want 1: %#v", len(args), args)
	}
	if got, ok := args[0].(string); !ok || got != value {
		t.Errorf("argument is %#v, want the string %q", args[0], value)
	}
}

// TestHostileFilterValuesAreNeverInSQL sweeps the values that break a builder
// which formats instead of binds — quotes and backslashes break the literal,
// whitespace runs used to be eaten by squash(), and non-ASCII proves nothing
// re-encodes the value on the way through.
//
// The primary assertion is that the SQL text is IDENTICAL to the text built for
// a benign value: the query must not vary with the value at all. That holds even
// for a value like `"` which is itself SQL punctuation (Postgres quotes its
// identifiers with it), where a substring search would be meaningless.
func TestHostileFilterValuesAreNeverInSQL(t *testing.T) {
	values := []string{
		"O'Brien",
		`'; DROP TABLE all_types; --`,
		`\`,
		`"`,
		"a\tb",
		"a   b",
		"ünïcode",
		`' OR '1'='1`,
	}

	for _, op := range []string{"=", ":"} {
		// The reference query: same shape, a value with nothing interesting in it.
		reference, _ := buildProbeQuery(t, fmt.Sprintf("t07_varchar_req %s %q", op, "benign"), false)

		for _, value := range values {
			t.Run(fmt.Sprintf("%s/%q", op, value), func(t *testing.T) {
				// strconv.Quote spells the value as a filter string literal; the
				// aip lexer unescapes it back to these exact bytes.
				query, args := buildProbeQuery(t, fmt.Sprintf("t07_varchar_req %s %s", op, strconv.Quote(value)), false)

				if query != reference {
					t.Errorf("the SQL text depends on the filter VALUE — some part of it was spliced in.\n got: %s\nwant: %s", query, reference)
				}
				// A one-character value is skipped here only because a lone `"` or
				// `\` can legitimately occur in the query's own syntax; the
				// text-identity check above already covers it.
				if len([]rune(value)) > 1 && strings.Contains(query, value) {
					t.Errorf("the filter value %q is in the SQL text:\n%s", value, query)
				}
				if n := strings.Count(query, "'"); n%2 != 0 {
					t.Errorf("SQL carries an odd number of single quotes (a literal is left open):\n%s", query)
				}

				if len(args) != 1 {
					t.Fatalf("got %d arguments, want 1: %#v", len(args), args)
				}
				want := value
				if op == ":" {
					want = "%" + value + "%"
				}
				if got, ok := args[0].(string); !ok || got != want {
					t.Errorf("argument is %#v, want the string %q", args[0], want)
				}
			})
		}
	}
}

// TestPlaceholdersAgreeWithArguments pins the invariant that makes binding safe
// in the first place: one marker per argument, in the order the arguments are
// listed. The clause walker emits text and binds values in the same traversal,
// which is the only reason the numbering can be right on Postgres — a builder
// that emitted a fragment before binding its value would silently shift every
// later ordinal onto the wrong argument.
func TestPlaceholdersAgreeWithArguments(t *testing.T) {
	const filter = `t07_varchar_req = "x" AND (t02_integer_req = 3 OR t07_varchar_req = "z")`
	query, args := buildProbeQuery(t, filter, false)

	if got := countPlaceholders(query); got != len(args) || got != 3 {
		t.Fatalf("%d placeholders for %d arguments (want 3 of each):\n%s\n%#v", got, len(args), query, args)
	}

	if got, ok := args[0].(string); !ok || got != "x" {
		t.Errorf("args[0] = %#v, want the string \"x\"", args[0])
	}
	if got, ok := args[1].(int64); !ok || got != 3 {
		t.Errorf("args[1] = %#v, want int64(3)", args[1])
	}
	if got, ok := args[2].(string); !ok || got != "z" {
		t.Errorf("args[2] = %#v, want the string \"z\"", args[2])
	}

	if ordinalPlaceholders() {
		// Numbered markers must appear once each and in ascending order, which
		// is what proves the ordinals were assigned in emission order.
		previous := -1
		for i := 1; i <= len(args); i++ {
			marker := placeholder(i)
			if n := strings.Count(query, marker); n != 1 {
				t.Fatalf("marker %s appears %d times, want once:\n%s", marker, n, query)
			}
			at := strings.Index(query, marker)
			if at < previous {
				t.Errorf("marker %s appears before %s — the ordinals do not follow the argument order:\n%s", marker, placeholder(i-1), query)
			}
			previous = at
		}
	}
}

// TestTimestampFilterBindsATime covers both spellings a timestamp comparison
// arrives in, and pins that the bound value is a time.Time rather than text: a
// driver renders a time.Time in the form the engine expects, while an RFC3339
// string is rejected outright by MySQL's literal parser.
func TestTimestampFilterBindsATime(t *testing.T) {
	want := time.Date(2024, time.January, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)

	for _, filter := range []string{
		// The conversion call: a CallExpr, so reading the constant off it
		// directly yields "" and the comparison became `> ''`.
		`t26_datetime_req > timestamp("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z")`,
		// The bare string: a constant, which the standard declarations accept
		// against a timestamp field through the _timestamp_string overloads.
		`t26_datetime_req > "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"`,
	} {
		query, args := buildProbeQuery(t, filter, false)
		if len(args) != 1 {
			t.Fatalf("%s: got %d arguments, want 1: %#v", filter, len(args), args)
		}
		got, ok := args[0].(time.Time)
		if !ok {
			t.Fatalf("%s: argument is %#v, want a time.Time", filter, args[0])
		}
		if !got.Equal(want) {
			t.Errorf("%s: bound %v, want %v", filter, got, want)
		}
		if strings.Contains(query, "2024") {
			t.Errorf("%s: the timestamp text is in the SQL:\n%s", filter, query)
		}
	}
}

// TestInvalidTimestampIsRejectedBeforeSQL records where a malformed timestamp is
// caught: aip's own type checker rejects it inside ParseFilter ("check call
// expr: invalid timestamp. Should be in RFC3339 format"), so it never reaches
// the query builder. That is the right layer — a filter the caller mis-spelled
// is a 400 from the transport's ParseFilter branch — and this assertion exists so
// that a change moving the check (or removing it) is noticed rather than silently
// letting an unparseable value through to the builder.
func TestInvalidTimestampIsRejectedBeforeSQL(t *testing.T) {
	const filter = `t26_datetime_req > "not-a-time"`
	parsed, err := filtering.ParseFilter(filterString(filter), probeDeclarations(t))
	if err != nil {
		return // rejected at parse time, as expected
	}

	// If aip ever accepts it, the builder must reject it — an unparseable
	// timestamp must never become part of a query.
	query, args, err := New().BuildListEntityQuery(
		context.Background(),
		probeRequest{filter: parsed, declarations: probeDeclarations(t)},
		main_entity.AllTypes{},
		false,
	)
	if err == nil {
		t.Errorf("%s was accepted by both the checker and the builder:\n%s\n%#v", filter, query, args)
	}
}

// TestLikeWildcardsPassThrough records today's contract for the `:` operator
// rather than an aspiration: `%` and `_` inside the caller's value stay
// WILDCARDS. Escaping them changes match semantics and was deliberately left out
// of the binding fix (it is a recorded follow-up); this assertion is what will
// fail, loudly and in one place, when that follow-up lands.
func TestLikeWildcardsPassThrough(t *testing.T) {
	_, args := buildProbeQuery(t, `t07_varchar_req : "50%"`, false)
	if len(args) != 1 {
		t.Fatalf("got %d arguments, want 1: %#v", len(args), args)
	}
	if got, ok := args[0].(string); !ok || got != "%50%%" {
		t.Errorf("argument is %#v, want %q — the value's own %% is not escaped", args[0], "%50%%")
	}
}

// TestNumericFiltersKeepTheirValue covers the two ways a float comparison used to
// lose its value: %f formatting rounded it to six decimals, and an int-spelled
// float was read with GetDoubleValue(), which returns 0 for an Int64 constant.
func TestNumericFiltersKeepTheirValue(t *testing.T) {
	_, args := buildProbeQuery(t, `t03_float_req > 0.000000123`, false)
	if len(args) != 1 {
		t.Fatalf("got %d arguments, want 1: %#v", len(args), args)
	}
	if got, ok := args[0].(float64); !ok || got != 0.000000123 {
		t.Errorf("argument is %#v, want float64(0.000000123) — %%f rendered this as 0.000000", args[0])
	}

	// `> 3` against a float field: an Int64 constant that has to survive as 3.
	_, args = buildProbeQuery(t, `t03_float_req > 3`, false)
	if len(args) != 1 {
		t.Fatalf("got %d arguments, want 1: %#v", len(args), args)
	}
	if got, ok := args[0].(float64); !ok || got != 3 {
		t.Errorf("argument is %#v, want float64(3) — an int-spelled float used to become 0", args[0])
	}
}

// TestNoByteSliceArguments sweeps every query this file builds. A []byte
// argument is rendered by go-sql-driver/mysql as _binary'...', which the server
// rejects for a JSON column with Error 3144 — so a builder that binds a JSON
// document must bind it as a string.
func TestNoByteSliceArguments(t *testing.T) {
	for _, filter := range probeFilters {
		for _, onlyCount := range []bool{false, true} {
			_, args := buildProbeQuery(t, filter, onlyCount)
			for i, a := range args {
				if _, isBytes := a.([]byte); isBytes {
					t.Errorf("%s (onlyCount=%v): args[%d] is a []byte; MySQL renders it as _binary'...' and rejects it (Error 3144)", filter, onlyCount, i)
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

// TestCountQuerySharesTheArguments pins that the count query built for a request
// carries the SAME arguments in the same order as its list query. They are built
// from one WHERE clause, and the count path returns early — so a value bound
// after that point would leave the count with fewer arguments than placeholders
// and fail at execution, not at build.
func TestCountQuerySharesTheArguments(t *testing.T) {
	for _, filter := range probeFilters {
		listQuery, listArgs := buildProbeQuery(t, filter, false)
		countQuery, countArgs := buildProbeQuery(t, filter, true)

		if len(countArgs) != len(listArgs) {
			t.Errorf("%s: count query has %d arguments, list query has %d", filter, len(countArgs), len(listArgs))
			continue
		}
		for i := range listArgs {
			if fmt.Sprintf("%T %v", countArgs[i], countArgs[i]) != fmt.Sprintf("%T %v", listArgs[i], listArgs[i]) {
				t.Errorf("%s: count args[%d] = %#v, list args[%d] = %#v", filter, i, countArgs[i], i, listArgs[i])
			}
		}
		if got := countPlaceholders(countQuery); got != len(countArgs) {
			t.Errorf("%s: count query has %d placeholders for %d arguments:\n%s", filter, got, len(countArgs), countQuery)
		}
		if got := countPlaceholders(listQuery); got != len(listArgs) {
			t.Errorf("%s: list query has %d placeholders for %d arguments:\n%s", filter, got, len(listArgs), listQuery)
		}
	}
}
